newsitem.title: USA: D'Amato welcomes Swiss fund move.
newsitem.headline: D'Amato welcomes Swiss fund move.

text.p: Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, who led a highly critical probe of Swiss dealings with the Nazis, on Friday hailed Switzerland's decision to set up a fund for Holocaust victims as an important first step in correcting a grave injustice.

But at a news conference at World Jewish Congress headquarters attended by Holocaust survivors, D'Amato hinted that more embarrassing revelations about Swiss wartime actions could be in the offing as the Clinton administration readies a report on whether the neutral nation tried to cover up purchases of looted Nazi gold.

A month after the then-Swiss president denounced the fund idea as "blackmail and extortion," Switzerland on Thursday reversed itself and said it would quickly establish a memorial fund to reimburse Holocaust victims or their survivors for money and other valuables they deposited in Swiss banks.
"The Swiss have taken an important first step. I am sorry that it has taken so long ... the call for justice has been vindicated," D'Amato said.

Holocaust survivors have tried for years to retrieve funds deposited by their families in secret Swiss bank accounts and have found themselves blocked by secrecy laws that required in some cases that they produce death certificates for people killed in Hitler's extermination camps.

D'Amato, the World Jewish Congress and other Jewish groups, backed by the Clinton administration, mounted an international campaign that was helped by the release of embarrassing documents from the U.S. National Archives that detailed extensive Swiss dealings with the Nazis.

Documents found in the archives indicated that Switzerland may have held up to $800 million in gold looted by the Nazis during the war. But in a 1946 treaty with Britain, France and the United States, the Swiss turned over $60 million.

D'Amato has called for the treaty to be renegotiated despite Swiss objections and the administration is expected to release a report late this month on the negotiations, using archive materials that were not previously known.

The senator said the report would show "that a terrible disservice was done." He also called on the Swiss to end their investigation of a 20-year-old bank guard who blew the whistle on a Swiss bank's shredding of wartime documents, saying the guard should be treated as a hero and the bank investigated.

Holocaust survivors at the news conference hailed the fund proposal but said it was coming very late in their lives. "It is a minute before midnight and justice has to be done now," said Benjamin Mead, head of the American Gathering of Holocaust Survivors.
